source: Grace Hill Company Pitch (August 2026), 30/3/30 structure. Supersedes the Bold v6 deck.
anchorPromise: Retention is the lever that raises revenue and lowers cost in the same quarter. Grace Hill gets teams there, and proves the number moved.
thirtySecond: NOI pressure never stops, and most operators are still chasing the wrong fix. Rent increases feel like the safe fix. They're not — management quality decides retention far more than price does, and that pressure on NOI never stops for owners and operators. Grace Hill connects the property data, benchmarks, and feedback nobody else has. Teams know what matters, act on it, and prove it improved. That's PerformanceHQ: issue to resolution.

threeMinute.gap: The gap is not data. It is what happens next. Most teams can see the issue. The harder part is resolving it, getting it done, and proving it worked.
threeMinute.close: Grace Hill is built for the work after the finding. AI is making findings cheaper. It is not making teams less busy. The value is knowing what to do and proving it worked.

loopNote: This used to be five steps. It is three, because that is how many an operator can actually hold a team to. Most tools stop at Know — they report. Some reach Act. paysTwice.thisYear: Residents who renew mean fewer turns, less vacancy, fewer concessions. Revenue goes up and turn cost goes down at the same time — the one lever that pays the property manager and the owner in the same quarter.
paysTwice.atExit: Durable NOI capitalizes. A one-time cost cut does not. A structural operating improvement survives the sale — and a buyer pays for it.
paysTwice.arithmetic: $100 of durable NOI per unit per year ÷ a 5% cap rate = $2,000 of asset value per unit = $600,000 on a single 300-unit asset.
paysTwice.note: Cap rate is illustrative. Ask theirs and redo the math live — it lands far harder in their numbers.

story.name: Denise
story.situation: Denise ran property operations across 40 properties.
story.pain: One property kept scoring low no matter which team rotated through it, and every review cited the same theme. Nobody could tell whether it was the people or the building.
story.impact: Once the pattern was clear enough to act on, her team made the case to ownership: a $100,000 renovation, approved in one meeting. NOI on that property has been climbing since.
story.point: Not every fix is training. Sometimes the property is the problem, not the people.
story.ask: What would it change to know that early?

stories.name: Patty
stories.role: VP of Training and Development, large operator, roughly 35,000 units
stories.situation: Her tools didn't talk to each other. Policies sat in paper handbooks, shopping was evaluated separately from development, and performance was tracked on a spreadsheet.
stories.pain: Leadership had no real-time view across the portfolio. Her teams didn't get information in time, and it showed up as inconsistent service and leasing.
stories.impact: Once it was connected, they stopped hunting for policies. Admins assigned targeted development, and her people found what they needed themselves.
stories.quote: Consolidation has been a game changer. It was a complete fresh start.
stories.point: The win was not a new feature. It was one place to look.
stories.ask: Where would that kind of visibility change how your team works?

stories.name: Walton
stories.role: Director of Property Management, roughly 2,500 A-class units
stories.useWhen: Can't make the case for spend
stories.situation: Data lived in different systems, so the team made it work manually.
stories.pain: An amenity space wasn't pulling its weight. Without knowing what residents actually wanted, his team couldn't justify upgrades, so it stayed under-invested while comps moved.
stories.impact: He went from guessing to acting with confidence, and secured a six-figure amenity investment from owners.
stories.point: The value was not the insight. It was that the insight was defensible enough to fund.
